chapters.name: Body Systems: Structure and Function
chapters.summary: The body's systems (muscular, skeletal, nervous, circulatory, lymphatic, and others), what they are made of, and what they do.
keyPoints: The muscular, skeletal, and nervous systems work together to make movement.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back to it.
The lymphatic system returns fluid to the blood and helps fight infection.
The sympathetic nervous system is fight or flight; the parasympathetic is rest and digest.

chapters.name: Tissue Injury, Repair, and Energetic Anatomy
chapters.summary: The four tissue types, the stages of tissue healing, and basic ideas of energetic anatomy such as meridians.
keyPoints: The four basic tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue.
Healing moves through inflammation, repair (proliferation), and remodeling.
Signs of inflammation are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function.
Meridians in traditional Chinese medicine are channels that energy (qi) is said to flow through.

chapters.name: Muscles: Attachments and Actions
chapters.summary: Major muscles, their origins and insertions, and what each muscle does.
keyPoints: The origin is usually the more fixed attachment; the insertion is the more movable one.
The agonist (prime mover) does the main action; the antagonist does the opposite action.
The rotator cuff muscles are the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis (SITS).
The hamstrings flex the knee and extend the hip.

chapters.name: Joints, Movement, and Proprioception
chapters.summary: Joint types, planes and directions of movement, and how the body senses position.
keyPoints: Flexion lowers the angle of a joint; extension increases it.
Abduction moves a part away from the midline; adduction moves it toward the midline.
Synovial joints such as the knee and shoulder move freely.
Muscle spindles sense stretch; Golgi tendon organs sense tension.

subjects.name: Pathology, Contraindications, Areas of Caution, Special Populations

chapters.name: Pathology and Contraindications
chapters.summary: Common conditions, when massage must be avoided, and when it must be adapted.
keyPoints: An absolute contraindication means no massage; a local contraindication means avoid that area.
Fever and contagious illness are reasons to reschedule a session.
Never massage an area with a suspected deep vein thrombosis (blood clot).
Ask about medications, because some change how a client feels pressure or heat.

chapters.name: Areas of Caution and Special Populations
chapters.summary: Endangerment sites and how to adapt sessions for pregnancy, older adults, and other groups.
keyPoints: Endangerment sites are areas where nerves and vessels lie near the surface, such as the front of the neck.
Avoid deep pressure in the popliteal fossa (back of the knee).
Pregnant clients are often positioned side-lying after the first trimester.
Older adults may have thin skin and fragile bones, so use lighter pressure.

subjects.name: Benefits and Effects of Soft Tissue Manipulation

chapters.name: Physiological and Psychological Effects
chapters.summary: How massage affects the body and mind, such as circulation, relaxation, and pain.
keyPoints: Massage can trigger the parasympathetic (relaxation) response.
Effleurage toward the heart helps venous and lymph return.
The gate control theory explains how touch can reduce the feeling of pain.
Massage can lower muscle tension and anxiety for many clients.

chapters.name: Techniques, Strokes, and Modalities
chapters.summary: Swedish strokes, other techniques, and when to use heat and cold.
keyPoints: The five basic Swedish strokes are effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement, and vibration.
Petrissage is kneading; tapotement is rhythmic tapping.
Cold (cryotherapy) narrows blood vessels and helps with fresh injuries.
Heat widens blood vessels and helps relax tight muscles.

chapters.name: Client Intake and Assessment
chapters.summary: Health history, interviews, posture and gait observation, and range of motion tests.
keyPoints: Take a health history before the first session and update it at each visit.
SOAP notes stand for Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan.
What the client says goes in Subjective; what you see or measure goes in Objective.
Active range of motion is done by the client; passive range of motion is done by the therapist.

chapters.name: Treatment Planning and Reassessment
chapters.summary: Setting goals with the client, choosing techniques, and checking results after the session.
keyPoints: Set treatment goals with the client, and make them clear and measurable.
Reassess after a session to see whether the plan is working.
Refer the client to a health care provider when a condition is outside your scope.
Get informed consent before you start and when you change the plan.

chapters.name: Ethics and Boundaries
chapters.summary: Professional boundaries, the therapeutic relationship, transference, and dual relationships.
keyPoints: The therapist is always responsible for keeping professional boundaries.
Transference is when a client projects feelings onto the therapist; countertransference is the reverse.
A dual relationship is having another role with a client, such as friend or business partner.
The client may stop the session at any time, and consent can be withdrawn.

chapters.name: Laws, Regulations, and Confidentiality
chapters.summary: Scope of practice, licensing rules, client records, and confidentiality.
keyPoints: Each state's massage practice act defines scope of practice and licensing rules.
Massage therapists do not diagnose medical conditions or prescribe medicine.
Keep client records private and share them only with written permission or as the law requires.
Draping must keep the client's private areas covered, as your state's rules require.

chapters.name: Safety, Sanitation, and Self-Care
chapters.summary: Hygiene, cleaning the table and linens, standard precautions, and body mechanics.
keyPoints: Wash hands before and after every session.
Use clean linens for every client.
Follow standard precautions for blood and body fluids.
Good body mechanics, such as a bow or warrior stance, protect the therapist.

chapters.name: Therapeutic Relationship and Business Practices
chapters.summary: Communication, policies, record keeping, and business and health care terms.
keyPoints: Give clear policies on cancellations, fees, and late arrivals before the first session.
Keep accurate business and client records.
Use plain language when you talk with clients.
Know common medical terms and abbreviations used in client records.
